title: That Church testimony is not faith's proper ground is proved by many arguments
source_text: XX. Quod autem res ita se habeat, neque testimonium et authoritas Ecclesiae sit fidei nostrae propria ratio, et praecipuum illud, in quod nostra de verbo Dei certitudo recumbit, probatur multis argumentis. Nam primo, si fides nostra tale fundamentum haberet, humana esset non divina: quia, scilicet, non divina veritate et authoritate, sed testimonio hominum niteretur. Deinde sequeretur fideles Deo credere, non propter ipsum, sed propter homines, et fidelium ipsorum respectu majorem esse hominum quam Dei authoritatem, quod valde absurdum est. Mutanda quoque esset fidei definitio. Nam, ex Doctorum omnium consensu, fides est assensus ille quem Deo loquenti praebemus. At sic per fidem, non tam Deo loquenti, quam hominibus crederemus. Neque fides esset assensus omnino firmus et infallibilis. Nulla enim humana veracitas tanta est, ut possit omnem falsi formidinem tollere.
pass_a_gloss: But that the matter stands so, and that the testimony and authority of the Church is not the proper ground of our faith, and that principal thing on which our certainty concerning God's Word rests, is proved by many arguments. For first, if our faith had such a foundation, it would be human, not divine: because, namely, it would rest not on divine truth and authority, but on the testimony of men. Next it would follow that believers believe God not because of God himself, but because of men, and that with respect to the believers themselves the authority of men is greater than God's, which is very absurd. The definition of faith would also have to be changed. For, by the consensus of all the Doctors, faith is that assent which we give to God speaking. But thus through faith we would believe not so much God speaking as men. Nor would faith be an assent altogether firm and infallible. For no human truthfulness is so great that it can remove every fear of falsehood.
pass_b_english: That matters stand this way — that the Church's testimony and authority is not the proper ground of our faith, not the chief thing on which our certainty about God's Word rests — is proved by many arguments. First: if our faith had that foundation, it would be human, not divine, because it would rest on men's testimony, not on divine truth and authority. Next it would follow that believers believe God not for God's sake but for men's, and that for the believers themselves men's authority is greater than God's — which is deeply absurd.

The definition of faith would have to change as well. By the consensus of all the Doctors, faith is the assent we give to God when he speaks. On that view, through faith we would be believing men more than God speaking. Nor would faith be an assent altogether firm and infallible. No human truthfulness is great enough to remove every fear of falsehood.
